sourceText: - **1.** Most people reject a 50/50 bet unless the possible gain is roughly twice the possible loss (Kahneman & Tversky, 1979; Tversky & Kahneman, 1992, estimated a loss-aversion ratio of about 2.25).
title: One risky offer
lens: compensation for a weighted loss

sourceText: - **2.** People judge outcomes as gains or losses relative to a reference point, not by total wealth (Kahneman & Tversky, 1979).
title: Where is the reference?
lens: the chosen reference point

sourceText: - **3.** Reflection effect: most prefer a sure $3,000 to an 80% chance of $4,000, yet prefer an 80% chance of losing $4,000 to a sure $3,000 loss (Kahneman & Tversky, 1979).
title: The gamble changes sign
lens: the sign of a lottery payoff

sourceText: - **4.** Diminishing sensitivity: the gap between $100 and $200 feels larger than the gap between $1,100 and $1,200 (Kahneman & Tversky, 1979).
title: Two equal cash gaps
lens: diminishing sensitivity in a curved scale

sourceText: - **5.** A meta-analysis of hundreds of loss-aversion estimates puts the average ratio near 2 (Brown, Imai, Vieider & Camerer, 2024).
title: Combine the loss estimates
lens: the weights behind a pooled estimate

sourceText: - **6.** Loss aversion is weaker or absent for small stakes and routine exchanges, a critique pressed by Gal & Rucker (2018).
title: A small routine exchange
lens: context dependence of the loss multiplier

sourceText: - **7.** New York cab drivers quit earlier on high-earning days, consistent with daily income targets (Camerer, Babcock, Loewenstein & Thaler, 1997). **\[contested\]** Farber (2005, 2015) found weaker evidence.
title: A busy day in the cab
lens: an income-target stopping rule

sourceText: - **10.** Teachers paid a bonus upfront that they had to return if targets were missed raised student math scores; an equal end-of-year bonus did not (Fryer, Levitt, List & Sadoff, 2012).
title: A bonus paid first
lens: the difference between a path and its final cash balance

sourceText: - **11.** Chinese factory teams worked harder when a bonus was framed as something they would lose rather than gain (Hossain & List, 2012).
title: Whose bonus is at risk?
lens: the reference used for a bonus

sourceText: - **13.** Retail investors realized 14.8% of their gains but only 9.8% of their losses (Odean, 1998).
title: Two piles of trades
lens: separate realization denominators

sourceText: - **14.** The tendency to sell winners too early and hold losers too long was named the disposition effect (Shefrin & Statman, 1985).
title: A winner and a loser
lens: the future gamble rather than its historical label

sourceText: - **15.** Investors who evaluate portfolios often feel losses more often, which can explain why stocks pay such a high premium over bonds (Benartzi & Thaler, 1995).
title: How often do you look?
lens: valuing the same cash path at different intervals

sourceText: - **17.** Professional futures traders showed this myopic loss aversion even more strongly than students (Haigh & List, 2005).
title: The trader's screen
lens: sensitivity to the assumed loss weight

sourceText: - **18.** Home-insurance customers paid about $100 a year to cut their deductible from $1,000 to $500, despite a claim rate under 5% (Sydnor, 2010).
title: A lower deductible
lens: the claim probability needed to offset a premium

sourceText: - **19.** Capuchin monkeys trading tokens for food avoided options framed as losses (Chen, Lakshminarayanan & Santos, 2006).
title: Tokens in two frames
lens: equivalent token outcomes

sourceText: - **20.** Brain regions that track value responded more steeply to potential losses than to equal gains (Tom, Fox, Trepel & Poldrack, 2007).
title: Two response slopes
lens: asymmetric slopes in an illustrative response curve

sourceText: - **21.** After a rigged wheel landed on 10 or 65, median estimates of the share of African countries in the UN were 25% and 45% (Tversky & Kahneman, 1974).
title: The wheel and the estimate
lens: the arbitrary starting point with fixed evidence

sourceText: - **22.** People estimating 8×7×6×5×4×3×2×1 in five seconds guessed a median 2,250; those shown 1×2×…×8 guessed 512. The answer is 40,320 (Tversky & Kahneman, 1974).
title: Which end of the product?
lens: the invariant product behind order-dependent guesses

sourceText: - **23.** Students with high final digits in their Social Security number bid 57–107% more for wine and chocolate (Ariely, Loewenstein & Prelec, 2003). **\[contested\]** Later replications found much smaller effects (Maniadis, Tufano & List, 2014).
title: A smaller later estimate
lens: how evidence weights affect an apparent replication gap

sourceText: - **25.** Experienced German judges who rolled loaded dice showing 3 or 9 proposed sentences of about 5 versus 8 months for the same case (Englich, Mussweiler & Strack, 2006).
title: Dice before a judgment
lens: an irrelevant number entering a decision rule

sourceText: - **26.** Asked whether Gandhi died before or after age 9 or age 140, people estimated about 50 and 67 (Strack & Mussweiler, 1997).
title: An implausible age cue
lens: the weight allowed to an implausible cue

sourceText: - **27.** Anchors work by making anchor-consistent information easier to recall (Strack & Mussweiler, 1997; Mussweiler & Strack, 1999).
title: Recall changes the mixture
lens: which information receives weight

sourceText: - **28.** The first offer in a negotiation strongly predicts the final price (Galinsky & Mussweiler, 2001).
title: The opening offer
lens: the opening number with unchanged outside evidence

sourceText: - **30.** Forewarning people about anchoring did not remove it (Wilson, Houston, Etling & Brekke, 1996).
title: A warning before the cue
lens: a reduction rather than elimination of anchoring

sourceText: - **31.** Anchoring replicated strongly across 36 labs, among the sturdiest effects tested (Klein et al., Many Labs 1, 2014).
title: Count the laboratory results
lens: the denominator behind a replication share

sourceText: - **33.** When people generate their own anchors, they stop adjusting too early, and adjust even less when distracted or drinking (Epley & Gilovich, 2001, 2006).
title: When does adjustment stop?
lens: the remaining distance after repeated adjustment

sourceText: - **34.** Mock jurors awarded larger damages when plaintiffs asked for more, even absurd amounts (Chapman & Bornstein, 1996).
title: A larger damages request
lens: the leverage of a request under a stated weighting rule

sourceText: - **35.** Showing a minimum payment on credit card statements lowered what people chose to repay (Stewart, 2009).
title: The displayed minimum
lens: interest versus a salient payment

sourceText: - **37.** Raising NYC taxi screens' default tip options raised average tips but also raised the share of riders who tipped nothing (Haggag & Paci, 2014).
title: Higher tips, fewer tippers?
lens: the extensive and intensive margins of tipping

sourceText: - **38.** At art auctions, an artwork's previous sale price anchors its next price (Beggs & Graddy, 2009).
title: The previous auction price
lens: the historical price held against current evidence

sourceText: - **39.** Economists' macro forecasts are anchored on recent data releases (Campbell & Sharpe, 2009).
title: A fresh data release
lens: the weight placed on recent information

sourceText: - **40.** Anchors that are obviously irrelevant still move answers, as long as they are attended to (Tversky & Kahneman, 1974; Strack & Mussweiler, 1997).
title: An unrelated number
lens: an irrelevant cue in an explicit model

sourceText: - **41.** "Asian disease" problem: 72% chose a sure plan saving 200 of 600 lives, but 78% chose the gamble when the same plan was described as 400 dying (Tversky & Kahneman, 1981).
title: Two descriptions of 600
lens: the saved and lost frames of one unchanged outcome

sourceText: - **42.** This gain/loss framing effect replicated across 36 labs (Klein et al., Many Labs 1, 2014).
title: A result across laboratories
lens: counting replications without inferring universality

sourceText: - **43.** A meta-analysis of risky-choice framing found a reliable, moderate effect (Kühberger, 1998).
title: A difference in standardized units
lens: the spread behind a standardized effect

sourceText: - **44.** Physicians favored surgery more when told of a 90% survival rate than a 10% mortality rate (McNeil, Pauker, Sox & Tversky, 1982).
title: Survival and mortality
lens: two complementary descriptions of one outcome

sourceText: - **46.** Framing comes in three kinds: risky-choice, attribute and goal framing, with different strengths (Levin, Schneider & Gaeth, 1998).
title: Same number, three frames
lens: outcome equivalence across labels

sourceText: - **47.** After losing a $10 bill, 88% would still buy a theater ticket; after losing the ticket itself, only 46% would buy another (Tversky & Kahneman, 1981).
title: A bill or a ticket
lens: the budget remaining after a second purchase

sourceText: - **48.** 68% would drive 20 minutes to save $5 on a $15 calculator, but only 29% to save $5 on a $125 one (Tversky & Kahneman, 1981).
title: A five-unit saving
lens: the denominator in a relative saving

sourceText: - **49.** Card companies pushed for price gaps to be called a "cash discount" rather than a "credit surcharge" (Thaler, 1980).
title: Cash discount or surcharge?
lens: the stated base price in a price frame

sourceText: - **51.** Junior economists registered early for a conference more often when the late fee was framed as a penalty than when the early fee was a discount (Gächter, Orzen, Renner & Starmer, 2009).
title: Register now or later
lens: the same price gap described from two bases

sourceText: - **52.** US Republicans were far more willing to pay a carbon fee labeled an "offset" than one labeled a "tax" (Hardisty, Johnson & Weber, 2010).
title: A fee with a different label
lens: the final bill rather than a label

sourceText: - **53.** About 72% chose an annuity when it was framed as consumption, but only 21% when framed as an investment (Brown, Kling, Mullainathan & Wrobel, 2008).
title: A stream or a lump sum
lens: the discounting of an identical payment stream

sourceText: - **56.** People often picked a bowl with 7 red beans in 100 over 1 in 10, preferring more winning items to better odds (Denes-Raj & Epstein, 1994).
title: Which bowl has better odds?
lens: winning tokens versus winning proportions

sourceText: - **57.** Bayesian reasoning jumped from about 16% to 46% correct when problems used natural frequencies instead of probabilities (Gigerenzer & Hoffrage, 1995).
title: Percentages or people?
lens: the denominator behind a descriptive accuracy comparison

sourceText: - **58.** Only 21% of gynecologists correctly said a positive mammogram means about a 1 in 10 chance of cancer (Gigerenzer et al., 2007).
title: How many estimates were right?
lens: the denominator in a reported accuracy share

sourceText: - **59.** Framing effects shrank when people made the choice in a foreign language (Keysar, Hayakawa & An, 2012).
title: A framing effect in context
lens: a context-dependent standardized contrast

sourceText: - **60.** Removing a discount is judged fairer than adding a surcharge, even for the same final price (Kahneman, Knetsch & Thaler, 1986).
title: Withdraw a discount
lens: the comparison price used by a description

sourceText: - **61.** Organ-donor consent ran 86–100% in opt-out European countries versus 4–28% in opt-in ones (Johnson & Goldstein, 2003).
title: Who is registered?
lens: registration rates and their comparison group

sourceText: - **62.** Online, 42% agreed to be donors under opt-in, 82% under opt-out and 79% when forced to choose (Johnson & Goldstein, 2003).
title: An active choice option
lens: the comparison arm in a choice-architecture example

sourceText: - **64.** Automatic 401(k) enrollment raised new hires' participation from about 37% to 86% (Madrian & Shea, 2001).
title: Automatically in the plan
lens: the participation-rate difference

sourceText: - **65.** Most auto-enrolled workers stayed at the 3% default rate, so some saved less than they would have chosen (Madrian & Shea, 2001).
title: The default contribution
lens: a contribution rate as well as enrollment

sourceText: - **66.** Employees tend to follow the "path of least resistance" across nearly every plan default (Choi, Laibson, Madrian & Metrick, 2004).
title: The path with less resistance
lens: which option receives the default weight

sourceText: - **68.** Making green electricity the default raised green contracts nearly tenfold in a German online experiment (Ebeling & Lotz, 2015).
title: A tenfold change from what?
lens: the base behind a large relative increase

sourceText: - **70.** A meta-analysis of 58 studies found defaults have a medium-to-large average effect, d ≈ 0.68 (Jachimowicz, Duncan, Weber & Johnson, 2019).
title: How large is the default gap?
lens: the unit used for an effect-size comparison

sourceText: - **71.** About 75% of Pennsylvania drivers kept a full-tort default, versus about 20% of New Jersey drivers who had to opt in (Johnson, Hershey, Meszaros & Kunreuther, 1993).
title: Different starting legal options
lens: choice shares under two stated defaults

sourceText: - **72.** Car buyers accepted more defaults when hard, many-option decisions came first in the configurator (Levav, Heitmann, Herrmann & Iyengar, 2010).
title: Hard choices come first
lens: the work required by a decision sequence

sourceText: - **73.** Nudges that make healthy food more convenient work better than those that only inform (Cadario & Chandon, 2020).
title: Make a choice easier
lens: the action cost in an illustrative convenience nudge

sourceText: - **74.** A meta-analysis found a moderate average nudge effect, d ≈ 0.43 (Mertens et al., 2022), but correcting for publication bias left little evidence of an overall effect (Maier et al., 2022).
title: What if missing studies differ?
lens: the contribution of less favorable evidence

sourceText: - **75.** Nudges tested by government nudge units raised outcomes 1.4 percentage points on average, versus 8.7 points in published academic papers (DellaVigna & Linos, 2022).
title: Academic and scaled effects
lens: absolute effect gaps across samples

sourceText: - **76.** Pre-scheduled flu-shot appointments raised vaccination from 33% to 45% (Chapman, Li, Colby & Yoon, 2010).
title: A prebooked appointment
lens: the comparison behind a participation lift

sourceText: - **77.** HIV testing rose from 38% (opt-in) to 51% (active choice) to 66% (opt-out) in an emergency department (Montoy, Dow & Kaplan, 2016).
title: Three testing invitations
lens: the invitation arm held against a common baseline

sourceText: - **79.** Health-plan inertia cost employees roughly $2,000 a year in foregone savings (Handel, 2013).
title: A plan that stays put
lens: the financial horizon of switching

sourceText: - **80.** In Sweden's 2000 pension reform about two-thirds actively picked funds; within a few years under 10% of new entrants did, and the default fund outperformed the average chosen portfolio (Cronqvist & Thaler, 2004).
title: An initial pension choice
lens: the composition of active and default choices

sourceText: - **81.** Preschoolers who waited longer for a second marshmallow later had higher SAT scores (Shoda, Mischel & Peake, 1990).
title: Waiting and family background
lens: a mixture that can create a pooled association

sourceText: - **82.** **\[contested\]** A larger, more diverse replication found the link about half as strong and mostly explained by family background (Watts, Duncan & Quan, 2018).
title: The same link after adjustment
lens: composition changes rather than a causal diagnosis

sourceText: - **83.** Many prefer $100 today over $110 tomorrow, yet prefer $110 in 31 days over $100 in 30 days, a preference reversal (Thaler, 1981; Ainslie, 1975).
title: Today and next month
lens: the extra weight applied when one option is immediate

sourceText: - **84.** Implied discount rates are far higher over short delays than long ones (Thaler, 1981).
title: One more day of waiting
lens: the delay under a hyperbolic discount rule

sourceText: - **85.** The "beta-delta" model captures this extra weight on the present (Laibson, 1997; O'Donoghue & Rabin, 1999).
title: The extra present-time weight
lens: the separate roles of present bias and ordinary discounting

sourceText: - **88.** In the Philippines 28% took up a locked savings account, and their savings rose 81% after a year (Ashraf, Karlan & Yin, 2006).
title: An account people may decline
lens: the share reached by a commitment offer

sourceText: - **89.** 74% chose fruit as a snack for next week, but 70% chose chocolate for right now (Read & van Leeuwen, 1998).
title: A snack now or later
lens: the timing in a stated temptation model

sourceText: - **90.** People pick highbrow films for later and lowbrow films for tonight (Read, Loewenstein & Kalyanaraman, 1999).
title: Tonight's film and next week's
lens: the time assigned to a delayed reward

sourceText: - **91.** Present bias shows up strongly for effort but weakly for money (Augenblick, Niederle & Sprenger, 2015).
title: Money or tomorrow's effort
lens: different model weights for different reward domains

sourceText: - **92.** A small, time-limited fertilizer discount at harvest raised Kenyan farmers' use about as much as much larger later subsidies (Duflo, Kremer & Robinson, 2011).
title: A discount with a deadline
lens: the final cost under a stated subsidy

sourceText: - **93.** More present-biased people carry more credit card debt (Meier & Sprenger, 2010).
title: Present spending, later balance
lens: the cash consequence of a smaller current payment

sourceText: - **95.** Gym visits and searches for "diet" spike after new weeks, months, birthdays and holidays, a "fresh start" effect (Dai, Milkman & Riis, 2014).
title: The start of a new period
lens: a planning boundary and a stated daily rate

sourceText: - **96.** People unaware of their own present bias procrastinate more than those who anticipate it (O'Donoghue & Rabin, 1999).
title: Do you anticipate the delay?
lens: anticipating a future reversal under an explicit rule

sourceText: - **97.** A commitment contract raised Filipino smokers' chances of passing a nicotine test at six months by 3–4 percentage points (Giné, Karlan & Zinman, 2010).
title: A contract and a later test
lens: an absolute percentage-point difference

sourceText: - **99.** Convertibles sell better on sunny days and four-wheel drives after snowstorms (Busse, Pope, Pope & Silva-Risso, 2015).
title: Today's weather in a choice
lens: a current-state cue weighted against long-run conditions

sourceText: - **100.** People who overrated their self-control exposed themselves to more temptation, and smokers among them relapsed more (Nordgren, van der Pligt & van Harreveld, 2009).
title: A forecast of self-control
lens: how much contrary evidence changes a belief

sourceText: - **101.** People sort money into mental accounts (rent, fun, savings) and treat each by different rules (Thaler, 1985).
title: Separate envelopes
lens: the cash made unavailable by a mental account

sourceText: - **102.** These accounts change real spending, not just how people describe it (Thaler, 1999).
title: A label with a spending rule
lens: a label’s effect under an explicit allocation rule

sourceText: - **104.** Dutch child benefits were spent more on children's clothing than equal income from other sources (Kooreman, 2000).
title: An income source and a category
lens: the stated fraction allocated to a spending category

sourceText: - **105.** An unconditional cash transfer merely labeled "for education" raised Moroccan school participation about as much as a conditional one (Benhassine et al., 2015).
title: Money labelled for education
lens: the restriction imposed by an illustrative budget label

sourceText: - **106.** Theater-goers who paid full price for season tickets attended more in the first half of the season than those given discounts (Arkes & Blumer, 1985).
title: A prepaid season ticket
lens: the unrecoverable past payment

sourceText: - **107.** NBA players drafted higher got more playing time than their performance justified (Staw & Hoang, 1995). **\[contested\]** Later work found weaker effects (Camerer & Weber, 1999).
title: Draft position and performance
lens: a composition explanation for a playing-time association

sourceText: - **109.** After a gain, people take more risk with the "house money" (Thaler & Johnson, 1990).
title: What counts as house money?
lens: the future gamble rather than the source of earlier money

sourceText: - **110.** After losses, people prefer gambles that offer a chance to break even, which is why long shots get more bets in the last race of the day (Thaler & Johnson, 1990; McGlothlin, 1956).
title: A chance to get back to zero
lens: the probability as well as the break-even prize

sourceText: - **112.** Paying hurts, and pre-paying or flat fees reduce that "pain of paying" (Prelec & Loewenstein, 1998).
title: When was the bill paid?
lens: the total payment under differently timed labels

sourceText: - **113.** People recall past spending less accurately when they paid by card or check than by cash (Soman, 2001).
title: Remembering earlier spending
lens: the denominator behind a recall score

sourceText: - **114.** Windfall money is gambled and spent more readily than earned money (Arkes et al., 1994).
title: A windfall in a new envelope
lens: the allocation rule applied to a windfall

sourceText: - **115.** Households spend a large share of tax refunds within the same quarter they arrive (Souleles, 1999).
title: A predictable refund arrives
lens: a buffer after a stated spending path

sourceText: - **116.** Consumption jumps when Social Security checks arrive, though income was fully predictable (Stephens, 2003).
title: The day the check arrives
lens: the cash remaining across a payment cycle

sourceText: - **117.** Food stamp recipients' calorie intake fell 10–15% over the month between payments (Shapiro, 2005).
title: A monthly food budget
lens: the shrinking remainder within a fixed payment cycle

sourceText: - **119.** People prefer to hear gains separately and losses bundled together (Thaler, 1985).
title: Two gains, one account
lens: valuing separate and combined changes on a curved scale

sourceText: - **120.** Wine bought years ago and drunk now often feels free, while breaking a bottle feels like a loss (Shafir & Thaler, 2006).
title: The bottle bought long ago
lens: the historical cost versus the remaining use decision

sourceText: - **121.** Students given a mug asked about $7.12 to sell it; those without one offered about $2.87 (Kahneman, Knetsch & Thaler, 1990).
title: Buying and selling the mug
lens: the size of a valuation gap

sourceText: - **122.** 89% of people given a mug kept it rather than swap for chocolate, and 90% given chocolate kept it (Knetsch, 1989).
title: Keep the gift or swap it?
lens: the role assigned before an exchange

sourceText: - **123.** Across studies, the median ratio of selling to buying price is about 2.6, and much higher for non-market goods (Horowitz & McConnell, 2002).
title: A ratio across valuations
lens: the unit behind a sell-to-buy ratio

sourceText: - **125.** **\[contested\]** With careful procedures the buy–sell gap can shrink or vanish (Plott & Zeiler, 2005).
title: Does the procedure change it?
lens: the sensitivity of a valuation gap to procedures

sourceText: - **126.** New and existing employees chose health plans very differently, with existing staff sticking to their current plan (Samuelson & Zeckhauser, 1988).
title: A familiar health plan
lens: the stated weight on a current option

sourceText: - **127.** Electricity customers preferred their current reliability-and-price plan, whichever it was (Hartman, Doane & Woo, 1991).
title: Your current electricity plan
lens: the opportunity cost of keeping a current plan

sourceText: - **128.** The longer people own something, the more they value it (Strahilevitz & Loewenstein, 1998).
title: Owning an object longer
lens: a chosen ownership-related weight in a toy valuation

sourceText: - **130.** Chimpanzees show an endowment effect for food (Brosnan et al., 2007).
title: A food item and an exchange
lens: the explicit exchange cost rather than a species-level claim

sourceText: - **131.** Hadza foragers with little market contact showed no endowment effect; more exposed Hadza did (Apicella, Azevedo, Christakis & Fowler, 2014).
title: Market experience and the gap
lens: a procedural contrast rather than a universal endowment claim

sourceText: - **133.** Many refuse to swap a lottery ticket for an identical one, even with a sweetener (Bar-Hillel & Neter, 1996).
title: Swap the lottery ticket?
lens: the payoff difference between equal-risk labels

sourceText: - **134.** Parents often reject a vaccine with lower risk than the disease, because harm from acting feels worse (Ritov & Baron, 1990).
title: Count both routes to harm
lens: a common denominator for acting and not acting

sourceText: - **135.** Harm caused by action is judged worse than equal harm caused by inaction (Spranca, Minsk & Baron, 1991).
title: Action and inaction in one table
lens: the arithmetic before assigning blame

sourceText: - **137.** Seniors in Medicare Part D often chose plans costing well above the cheapest equivalent (Abaluck & Gruber, 2011).
title: An equivalent plan costs less
lens: the horizon of avoidable plan costs

sourceText: - **138.** Most TIAA-CREF participants never changed their retirement allocation over their careers (Samuelson & Zeckhauser, 1988).
title: An allocation that never moves
lens: the weight on an unchanged allocation

sourceText: - **139.** There is no loss aversion for money handed over in routine purchases (Novemsky & Kahneman, 2005).
title: A routine purchase reference
lens: the assumed loss weight in a routine exchange

sourceText: - **140.** People given a lottery ticket demanded far more to sell it than others would pay to buy one (Knetsch & Sinden, 1984).
title: Who holds the lottery ticket?
lens: the selling and buying roles for the same object

sourceText: - **141.** A display of 24 jams drew more shoppers than 6 jams (60% vs 40%), but only 3% bought versus 30% (Iyengar & Lepper, 2000).
title: More visitors, fewer purchases?
lens: the two denominators in a choice funnel

sourceText: - **142.** **\[contested\]** A meta-analysis found the average choice-overload effect is close to zero, with large variation (Scheibehenne, Greifeneder & Todd, 2010).
title: An average near zero
lens: heterogeneity behind a pooled overload estimate

sourceText: - **143.** Overload does appear when choices are complex, preferences unclear, or people want to decide fast (Chernev, Böckenholt & Goodman, 2015).
title: How complex is the menu?
lens: the dimensions compared rather than option count alone

sourceText: - **144.** Each additional 10 funds in a 401(k) plan lowered participation 1.5–2 percentage points (Iyengar, Huberman & Jiang, 2004).
title: A larger retirement menu
lens: the absolute participation gap in a toy menu comparison

sourceText: - **145.** Investors split money evenly across whatever funds are offered, so the share in stocks tracks the share of stock funds (Benartzi & Thaler, 2001).
title: More stock funds on the menu
lens: the exposure created by equal allocation over menu items

sourceText: - **146.** People choose more variety when picking several items in advance than one at a time (Simonson, 1990; Read & Loewenstein, 1995).
title: A basket chosen all at once
lens: the menu composition of a planned basket

sourceText: - **147.** Israeli parole boards' favorable rulings fell from about 65% to near zero before food breaks (Danziger, Levav & Avnaim-Pesso, 2011). **\[contested\]** Case ordering may explain much of it (Weinshall-Margel & Shapard, 2011; Glöckner, 2016).
title: Cases before a break
lens: a possible ordering explanation for a time-of-day pattern

sourceText: - **148.** Adding an extreme option makes the middle option more popular, the compromise effect (Simonson, 1989).
title: An option in the middle
lens: a stated net comparison after the menu changes

sourceText: - **149.** Adding a clearly inferior "decoy" boosts the option it most resembles (Huber, Payne & Puto, 1982).
title: Add an inferior option
lens: strictly worse attributes versus a genuine tradeoff

sourceText: - **150.** **\[contested\]** Decoy effects are weaker or absent with real products and pictures rather than numeric tables (Frederick, Lee & Baskin, 2014).
title: Numbers or real products?
lens: the assumptions behind a numerical dominance claim

sourceText: - **152.** People pay to delay a choice until uncertainty resolves, even when they would choose the same either way (Tversky & Shafir, 1992).
title: Pay to wait for a decision
lens: the cost of delay when final outcomes are unchanged

sourceText: - **153.** Most employees at a large firm picked health plans that were strictly worse than another option, overpaying hundreds of dollars a year (Bhargava, Loewenstein & Sydnor, 2017).
title: A plan that costs more
lens: equal stated benefits with unequal costs

sourceText: - **154.** "Maximizers" got jobs paying about 20% more than "satisficers" but felt worse about them (Iyengar, Wells & Schwartz, 2006).
title: A better salary and what else?
lens: the salary percentage before inferring satisfaction

sourceText: - **156.** Simple one-click "quick enrollment" raised 401(k) participation by 10–20 percentage points (Beshears, Choi, Laibson & Madrian, 2013).
title: Enrollment with one click
lens: the absolute change in a toy enrollment comparison

sourceText: - **158.** Speed-dating events with more varied candidates led people to rely on simpler criteria like height and job (Lenton & Francesconi, 2010).
title: More candidates, fewer criteria
lens: the computation saved by using fewer attributes

sourceText: - **160.** Simplifying choice can raise take-up without removing any options (Beshears et al., 2013; Bettinger et al., 2012).
title: Simplify without deleting options
lens: the cost per comparison with an unchanged menu

sourceText: - **161.** In the first ultimatum games, the most common offer was half the pie, and low offers were often rejected (Güth, Schmittberger & Schwarze, 1982).
title: An offer that may be rejected
lens: the offer and the stated acceptance probability

sourceText: - **162.** Offers below about 20% of the pie are rejected roughly half the time (Camerer, 2003).
title: Keep more, risk the whole pie
lens: the expected payoff rather than the retained share alone

sourceText: - **164.** Societies more integrated into markets make fairer offers (Henrich et al., 2010).
title: Compare groups of offers
lens: composition before a society-level causal conclusion

sourceText: - **165.** Offers stay near 40–50% even at stakes worth months of wages (Cameron, 1999), but rejections fall as stakes grow very large (Andersen, Ertaç, Gneezy, Hoffman & List, 2011).
title: The same fraction at higher stakes
lens: the stated acceptance rule and the monetary scale

sourceText: - **166.** In dictator games, people give away about 20% on average, with many giving nothing or half (Forsythe, Horowitz, Savin & Sefton, 1994).
title: One allocator, two recipients
lens: the cash allocation under a chosen gift

sourceText: - **167.** A meta-analysis of 616 dictator treatments found average giving of about 28% (Engel, 2011).
title: What does average giving mean?
lens: the population behind a stated average giving fraction

sourceText: - **168.** Giving drops when even the experimenter cannot see who gave what (Hoffman, McCabe, Shachat & Smith, 1994).
title: Who can observe the allocation?
lens: the supplied allocation rather than an inferred motive

sourceText: - **171.** About a third of people paid $1 to exit a $10 dictator game without the recipient ever knowing (Dana, Cain & Dawes, 2006).
title: Pay to leave the game
lens: the monetary cost of exit

sourceText: - **172.** Inequity-aversion models explain these results by people disliking unequal payoffs (Fehr & Schmidt, 1999; Bolton & Ockenfels, 2000).
title: Money and an inequality penalty
lens: the difference between cash and model utility

sourceText: - **173.** Capuchin monkeys refused cucumber after seeing a partner get grapes for the same task (Brosnan & de Waal, 2003).
title: A different reward next door
lens: the comparison payoff in a stated inequality model

sourceText: - **174.** 82% said raising snow-shovel prices after a storm was unfair (Kahneman, Knetsch & Thaler, 1986).
title: The price after the storm
lens: the cash change before a fairness judgment

sourceText: - **175.** About 60% of uninvolved observers paid to punish stingy dictators (Fehr & Fischbacher, 2004).
title: A costly punishment rule
lens: the size and probability of a sanction

sourceText: - **176.** Unfair offers activate the anterior insula, linked to disgust (Sanfey et al., 2003).
title: A model response to an unequal split
lens: a payoff-based proxy rather than a brain measurement

sourceText: - **177.** Disrupting the right prefrontal cortex with magnetic stimulation made people accept more unfair offers (Knoch et al., 2006).
title: Acceptance and the offered share
lens: the assumed response probability with a fixed offer

sourceText: - **178.** Dislike of unequal splits develops between ages 3 and 8 (Fehr, Bernhard & Rockenbach, 2008).
title: Change the inequality weight
lens: the parameter in an illustrative preference rule

sourceText: - **179.** University of California staff who learned they earned below their unit's median reported lower satisfaction and more job search (Card, Mas, Moretti & Saez, 2012).
title: Where do coworkers set the bar?
lens: the comparison wage rather than the absolute wage

sourceText: - **181.** In the trust game, senders gave about half their money to strangers, and many receivers returned at least that much (Berg, Dickhaut & McCabe, 1995).
title: Money sent and money returned
lens: the two decisions inside a trust game

sourceText: - **182.** Across 162 replications, senders send about 50% and receivers return about 37% of what they hold (Johnson & Mislin, 2011).
title: A return percentage of what?
lens: the recipient pot as the return denominator

sourceText: - **183.** In public goods games, people start by contributing 40–60% but fall to about 10% by the final rounds (Ledyard, 1995).
title: Contributions across rounds
lens: the public-good payoff under two contribution levels

sourceText: - **184.** Letting players punish free riders drives contributions up toward full cooperation (Fehr & Gächter, 2000, 2002).
title: A sanction changes the payoff
lens: the enforcement probability in a payoff rule

sourceText: - **186.** About half of people are conditional cooperators and about a third are free riders (Fischbacher, Gächter & Fehr, 2001).
title: Conditional contributors and others
lens: the composition of an illustrative contributor population

sourceText: - **187.** When a public goods game restarts, contributions jump back up (Andreoni, 1988).
title: A public-goods game restarts
lens: the contribution level after a stated restart

sourceText: - **188.** A nasal spray of oxytocin raised trust (Kosfeld et al., 2005). **\[contested\]** Later studies mostly failed to replicate it (Nave, Camerer & McCullough, 2015).
title: A later estimate of trust
lens: the effect of less favorable evidence on a pooled estimate

sourceText: - **189.** In lab labor markets, higher wages drew more effort, a "gift exchange" (Fehr, Kirchsteiger & Riedl, 1993).
title: A wage and an effort schedule
lens: the output scale in a supplied effort rule

sourceText: - **191.** A small gift in a charity mailing raised donation rates 17%; a larger gift raised them 75% (Falk, 2007).
title: A gift in the mailing
lens: the baseline in a relative response comparison

sourceText: - **192.** A gift of a thermos raised workers' output about 25%, an equal cash bonus did nothing, and a wage cut lowered output about 20% (Kube, Maréchal & Puppe, 2012).
title: A gift, cash, or a wage cut
lens: the sign and denominator of an output change

sourceText: - **193.** Waiters who gave a mint with the bill got higher tips, and more still when the mint seemed a personal extra (Strohmetz et al., 2002).
title: A mint and a bill
lens: the tip rule in an illustrative gratuity calculation

sourceText: - **195.** Tit-for-tat won Axelrod's repeated prisoner's dilemma tournaments (Axelrod, 1980).
title: Cooperate again tomorrow?
lens: the value assigned to future cooperation

sourceText: - **196.** Cooperation in repeated games emerges mainly when it is both an equilibrium and not too risky (Dal Bó & Fréchette, 2011).
title: A future that might end
lens: the continuation weight required by a repeated-game comparison

sourceText: - **197.** Groups that could make agreements and sanction each other managed shared resources well (Ostrom, Walker & Gardner, 1992; Ostrom, 1990).
title: A rule for a shared resource
lens: the common-pool payoff under two specified rules

sourceText: - **198.** On the TV show *Golden Balls*, about 53% of contestants chose to split, even with large sums at stake (van den Assem, van Dolder & Thaler, 2012).
title: How many choose to split?
lens: the descriptive share rather than a theory of motives

sourceText: - **200.** Countries with higher trust have higher growth (Knack & Keefer, 1997; Zak & Knack, 2001), though the evidence is correlational.
title: Trust and growth in a sample
lens: composition before a cross-country causal interpretation

sourceText: - **201.** In Asch's line-judgment studies, people went along with an obviously wrong group about a third of the time, and about 75% conformed at least once (Asch, 1951, 1956).
title: How many judgments changed?
lens: a person-level versus a trial-level denominator

sourceText: - **202.** Hotel towel reuse rose from 35% to 44% with a "most guests reuse" sign, and to 49% when the norm referred to guests in the same room (Goldstein, Cialdini & Griskevicius, 2008).
title: A message about other guests
lens: the reference group used for a descriptive rate contrast

sourceText: - **203.** Home Energy Reports comparing households to neighbors cut electricity use about 2% (Allcott, 2011).
title: Two percent of a household bill
lens: the baseline behind a relative energy change

sourceText: - **204.** Those savings persisted for years when the reports continued (Allcott & Rogers, 2014).
title: A small change over years
lens: the duration of a persistent annual saving

sourceText: - **206.** UK tax letters saying "9 out of 10 people pay on time" raised on-time payment several percentage points (Hallsworth, List, Metcalfe & Vlaev, 2017).
title: A letter and on-time payment
lens: the comparison behind a small percentage-point lift

sourceText: - **208.** People litter more in an already littered place (Cialdini, Reno & Kallgren, 1990).
title: A clean place and a littered one
lens: the mixture behind a contextual association

sourceText: - **209.** Graffiti on a wall doubled littering from 33% to 69%, and visible disorder doubled theft of an envelope with money from 13% to 27% (Keizer, Lindenberg & Steg, 2008).
title: Two rates in a disorder study
lens: the distinction between a ratio and a percentage-point change

sourceText: - **210.** A mailer telling voters their neighbors would see who voted raised turnout 8.1 percentage points (Gerber, Green & Larimer, 2008).
title: Who can see that you voted?
lens: the absolute turnout difference in a toy comparison

sourceText: - **211.** A Facebook message showing friends who had voted generated an estimated 340,000 extra votes (Bond et al., 2012).
title: A small effect at large scale
lens: the population needed to turn a small rate into a count

sourceText: - **212.** A letter telling England's top antibiotic prescribers they prescribed more than peers cut prescriptions 3.3% (Hallsworth et al., 2016).
title: Fewer prescriptions from what base?
lens: the baseline used by a relative reduction

sourceText: - **213.** Peer comparison emails cut inappropriate antibiotic prescribing about 5 percentage points (Meeker et al., 2016).
title: A five-point reduction
lens: the denominator behind percentage points

sourceText: - **214.** Students wrongly believed peers were more comfortable with heavy drinking than they were (Prentice & Miller, 1993).
title: What do classmates believe?
lens: a perceived norm held against contrary information

sourceText: - **216.** Telling low-income workers how much peers saved made some of them less likely to enroll (Beshears, Choi, Laibson, Madrian & Milkman, 2015).
title: Peers' saving and your default
lens: the assumed default weight rather than a universal peer response

sourceText: - **217.** Telling students that 64% rather than 46% of peers gave to a fund slightly raised giving (Frey & Meier, 2004).
title: Which peer share was shown?
lens: the numerical content of a descriptive social norm

sourceText: - **218.** Telling public-radio donors that another caller gave $300 raised their gift about 12% (Shang & Croson, 2009).
title: Another caller's donation
lens: the baseline in a relative donation increase

sourceText: - **220.** Randomly assigned college roommates influence each other's grades and social choices, though modestly (Sacerdote, 2001).
title: Roommates in a toy sample
lens: composition and assignment before a peer-effect conclusion

sourceText: - **221.** 93% of US student drivers rated themselves above the median in skill (Svenson, 1981).
title: Who can be above the median?
lens: a logical ceiling on simultaneous rank claims

sourceText: - **222.** The weakest performers on logic and grammar tests, scoring around the 12th percentile, guessed they were near the 62nd (Kruger & Dunning, 1999). **\[contested\]** Part of the pattern is a statistical artifact (Nuhfer et al., 2016).
title: A rank and its self-estimate
lens: the signed rank gap without diagnosing its cause

sourceText: - **223.** Ranges people gave with 98% confidence missed the true answer far more than 2% of the time, often 40% or more (Alpert & Raiffa, 1982).
title: A narrow interval misses
lens: the realized miss count behind a confidence claim

sourceText: - **224.** Stock returns fell inside CFOs' 80% confidence intervals only 36% of the time (Ben-David, Graham & Harvey, 2013).
title: An interval that claims eighty
lens: the gap between claimed and observed coverage

sourceText: - **225.** Households that traded most earned 11.4% a year versus 17.9% for the market (Barber & Odean, 2000).
title: An active trader's return
lens: the accumulation of an annual return difference

sourceText: - **226.** Men traded 45% more than women, lowering their net returns more (Barber & Odean, 2001).
title: More trades from what baseline?
lens: the trading count behind a relative increase

sourceText: - **227.** Overconfident CEOs make more acquisitions, and markets react worse to them (Malmendier & Tate, 2005, 2008).
title: Acquisitions in different groups
lens: a composition explanation for an executive-level association

sourceText: - **228.** 81% of new entrepreneurs put their own odds of success at 70% or higher, and a third said 100% (Cooper, Woo & Dunkelberg, 1988).
title: A founder's success forecast
lens: the distance between a claim and a toy outcome frequency

sourceText: - **230.** Students predicted finishing their theses in 33.9 days; it took 55.5 on average (Buehler, Griffin & Ross, 1994).
title: The thesis finish date
lens: the planned duration as the overrun denominator

sourceText: - **231.** Nine in ten large infrastructure projects run over budget, with rail averaging about 45% overruns (Flyvbjerg, Holm & Buhl, 2002).
title: A rail budget changes
lens: the absolute budget behind a percentage overrun

sourceText: - **232.** 94% of university professors rated themselves above average at their job (Cross, 1977).
title: Above which average?
lens: the distinction between a mean and a median

sourceText: - **233.** People are overconfident on hard questions and underconfident on easy ones (Lichtenstein & Fischhoff, 1977).
title: Hard questions and easy ones
lens: the direction of a calibration gap across difficulty

sourceText: - **236.** Of three kinds of overconfidence, being too sure of one's precision is the most persistent (Moore & Healy, 2008).
title: Precision on paper
lens: the realized coverage of a stated interval procedure

sourceText: - **237.** Students rated their own chances of good life events higher, and bad ones lower, than their peers' (Weinstein, 1980).
title: Good and bad possibilities
lens: the direction and weight of a belief update

sourceText: - **238.** People update beliefs more after good news about their risks than bad news (Sharot, Korn & Dolan, 2011).
title: The same size of news
lens: different weights on equally sized news

sourceText: - **239.** Truck drivers kept overestimating their future productivity, even with experience (Hoffman & Burks, 2020).
title: Tomorrow's productivity forecast
lens: the calibration of repeated performance forecasts

sourceText: - **241.** 85% judged "Linda is a feminist bank teller" more likely than "Linda is a bank teller", which is logically impossible (Tversky & Kahneman, 1983).
title: A description adds a condition
lens: the subset relationship behind a conjunction

sourceText: - **242.** Physicians made the same conjunction error with medical scenarios (Tversky & Kahneman, 1983).
title: Two clinical conditions in a toy set
lens: the probability of a subset rather than a stereotype

sourceText: - **243.** People ignored whether a sample was 30% or 70% engineers when judging a person from a short description (Kahneman & Tversky, 1973).
title: Engineers in two populations
lens: the base-rate mixture behind a description

sourceText: - **244.** In the cab problem, the typical answer was 80% when the correct probability was about 41% (Tversky & Kahneman, 1982).
title: The witness and the cab fleet
lens: the gap between an estimate and a stated benchmark

sourceText: - **246.** People overestimate dramatic causes of death like tornadoes and underestimate common ones like diabetes (Lichtenstein et al., 1978).
title: Which risks were recalled?
lens: the denominator in a stated recall task

sourceText: - **248.** Fear of flying after 9/11 shifted Americans to driving, causing an estimated 1,600 extra road deaths (Gigerenzer, 2006).
title: Switching routes after a scare
lens: the expected risk of both available routes

sourceText: - **249.** Early research found no "hot hand" in basketball (Gilovich, Vallone & Tversky, 1985). **\[contested\]** Correcting a subtle statistical bias suggests a hot hand does exist (Miller & Sanjurjo, 2018).
title: A streak in a small sample
lens: the sampling protocol before a claim about a hot hand

sourceText: - **250.** Asylum judges, loan officers and baseball umpires are less likely to rule the same way twice in a row, a gambler's fallacy (Chen, Moskowitz & Shue, 2016).
title: Does the last decision predict next?
lens: the independence assumption behind a sequence of decisions
